pharm: Competitively blocks histamine H1 receptors, reducing histamine-mediated allergic responses such as itching, wheal formation and increased vascular permeability
quick: Oral 1 mg three times daily (drops/tablets); modified-release 4 mg once or twice daily; topical gel applied to affected skin
Oral forms may be taken with or without food
Avoid especially in the first trimester unless clearly necessary
Not recommended; antihistamines may pass into milk and affect the infant
Use with caution; no specific adjustment well established
Use with caution in hepatic impairment
summary: Dimethindene (dimetindene) maleate is a first-generation H1-antihistamine used to relieve allergic conditions such as urticaria, allergic rhinitis, pruritus of various causes, food and drug allergies, and insect bites, and as a topical gel for localised itching. It competitively antagonises histamine at H1 receptors, reducing itching, wheal-and-flare reactions and other histamine-mediated symptoms; like other sedating antihistamines it crosses into the CNS and can cause drowsiness, and it has anticholinergic effects. Oral forms (drops or tablets) are typically dosed as 1 mg three times daily, with a modified-release formulation given once or twice daily; a topical gel is applied to affected skin. Dimethindene is NOT approved by the US FDA; it is marketed in Europe and other regions, so dosing and indications here are based on EMA/SmPC and equivalent sources.
indications: Symptomatic relief of allergic conditions: urticaria, allergic (seasonal and perennial) rhinitis, food and drug allergies
Pruritus of various origins (except that due to cholestasis) including from chickenpox, insect bites and eczema
Topical gel: local relief of itching and minor skin irritation (insect bites, sunburn, urticaria, minor burns)

dosage.d: 1 mg three times daily (e.g. 20 drops three times daily, or 1 mg tablet)
dosage.t: By mouth, with or without food
dosage.n: Total around 3-6 mg/day per local labelling

dosage.d: 4 mg once or twice daily (modified-release capsule)
dosage.t: Swallow whole, often at night and/or morning
dosage.n: Designed for prolonged effect/reduced dosing frequency

dosage.d: Apply 0.1% gel to the affected area 2-4 times daily
dosage.n: Avoid large areas, broken skin and sun exposure of treated skin

admin: Take oral drops/tablets as directed; the modified-release form is often taken at night to reduce daytime drowsiness
Swallow modified-release capsules whole - do not crush or chew
Apply topical gel as a thin layer to affected skin; avoid extensive areas or broken/sun-exposed skin
Avoid alcohol and caution with other sedatives because of additive drowsiness
Warn patients about driving or operating machinery until effects are known
Use lowest effective dose and shortest duration needed for symptom control
moa: Dimethindene is a competitive antagonist at peripheral and central histamine H1 receptors. By blocking H1 receptors it reduces the effects of histamine released in allergic reactions - decreasing pruritus, capillary permeability, wheal-and-flare responses and smooth-muscle effects. As a first-generation (sedating) antihistamine it crosses the blood-brain barrier, producing CNS depression/drowsiness, and it also has anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) and some local anaesthetic activity. The topical gel provides local antipruritic effect at the application site.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dimethindene or formulation components
Neonates and premature infants (oral; per labelling)
relative: Urinary retention / prostatic hypertrophy / bladder-neck obstruction
Significant respiratory disease (asthma) - caution with antimuscarinic drying
Epilepsy; elderly (increased sensitivity to sedation and anticholinergic effects)
monitor: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision)

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established. Dimethindene should be avoided during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, and used only if clearly necessary and after weighing the benefit against the risk.
lact: Antihistamines can pass into breast milk and may cause effects (such as irritability or drowsiness) in the infant, and may reduce milk production. Dimethindene is not recommended during breastfeeding.
renal: There is limited specific guidance; use with caution in renal impairment, as for other sedating antihistamines, and monitor for excessive sedation or anticholinergic effects.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment, as metabolism may be altered; monitor for increased sedation and adverse effects.

major: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, hypnotics, sedating antidepressants) - additive sedation and respiratory/CNS depression
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - may intensify and prolong anticholinergic effects
moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (tricyclic antidepressants, antispasmodics, some antiparkinson agents) - additive antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation)
minor: May mask warning signs of ototoxicity from other drugs
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no significant food interaction
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive central nervous system depression
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress skin reactions to allergy (skin-prick) testing - stop several days before such tests

common: Drowsiness/sedation, especially at the start of treatment
serious: Marked CNS depression or paradoxical excitation (especially in children/elderly)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma precipitation in susceptible patients
emergency: Severe CNS depression or respiratory depression (overdose)

monitoring: Degree of sedation and ability to perform skilled tasks/driving
Anticholinergic effects (urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision)
Symptom control and ongoing need for treatment
Intraocular pressure in patients at risk of glaucoma
counsel: This medicine can make you drowsy - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Do not drink alcohol or take other sedatives with it, as this increases drowsiness
You may get a dry mouth, blurred vision or difficulty passing urine - tell your doctor if these are troublesome
If using the gel, apply a thin layer and keep treated skin out of the sun
Stop the medicine a few days before any allergy skin testing and tell the tester you have used it
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding
pk: Antihistamine effect within about 30 minutes of an oral dose
Plasma concentrations peak around 2 hours after oral dosing (immediate-release)
Several hours per immediate-release dose; modified-release provides prolonged effect for once/twice-daily dosing
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture per product labelling
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - marketed in Europe and other regions; dosing/indications based on EMA/SmPC and equivalent sources
First-generation (sedating) antihistamine - warn about drowsiness and avoid alcohol/other CNS depressants
Has anticholinergic effects - caution in glaucoma, prostatic enlargement and the elderly
Stop several days before allergy skin testing, which it can suppress
A topical 0.1% gel form exists for localised itching; avoid large areas, broken skin and sun exposure
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose can cause CNS depression (drowsiness, coma) or, particularly in children, CNS stimulation with excitation, hallucinations and seizures, together with anticholinergic features (dry mouth, flushing, dilated pupils, urinary retention, tachycardia) and, in severe cases, respiratory and cardiovascular depression. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive with airway/respiratory support, activated charcoal if appropriate, and symptomatic management of seizures and cardiovascular effects.
